summary: Describes using one RSVP reservation to represent many reservations across a transit region, similar to virtual paths in ATM. It covers creating, classifying, sizing, and releasing the aggregate.

plainLanguage.summary: RSVP aggregation lets edge routers represent many individual reservations with a smaller set of shared reservations inside a network region. The interior routers process those shared reservations instead of tracking every end-to-end flow.

questions: how does rsvp scale across a diffserv network
subtitle: How edge routers combine many RSVP reservations into fewer reservations across a transit region.

tldr.problem: RSVP stores reservation state and processes messages for each flow at every router, creating scaling costs inside a transit network.
tldr.mechanism: An aggregator hides selected end-to-end RSVP messages from interior routers and establishes an aggregate reservation with a deaggregator. DSCPs classify traffic within the region.
tldr.outcome: Interior routers can keep state for aggregate reservations rather than each end-to-end flow. RFC 3175 was later updated by RFC 5350.

today: RFC 3175 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2001. It was updated by RFC 5350 and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Aggregate Reservations
sections.content:
Each RSVP reservation requires message exchanges, computation and memory at every router along its path. RFC 3175 combines several end-to-end (E2E) reservations that cross the same region and share ingress and egress routers into one aggregate reservation.

Aggregation reduces the number of reservation records inside the region, but it also reduces isolation between flows. One flow may experience delay from another flow's bursts.
sections.plainLanguage: Tracking every reservation at every router uses resources. Aggregation lets the routers inside a region track a shared reservation for several flows.

sections.title: The Aggregator and Deaggregator
sections.content:
The aggregator is the first router that processes an E2E Path message as it enters the aggregation region. The deaggregator is the last router that processes it as it leaves. Routers between them forward the E2E message without keeping its RSVP state.

The deaggregator chooses which aggregate reservation carries an E2E flow, based on the network administrator's policy. It has the E2E Resv information needed to make that choice and tells the aggregator which mapping to use.
sections.plainLanguage: The aggregator is the entrance router, and the deaggregator is the exit router. The exit chooses the shared reservation for each flow and informs the entrance.

sections.title: Hiding E2E Messages and Marking Traffic
sections.content:
On entry, the aggregator changes the IP protocol number in E2E Path, PathTear and ResvConf messages from RSVP 46 to RSVP-E2E-IGNORE 134. Interior routers forward these messages as ordinary IP datagrams rather than processing them as RSVP. The deaggregator restores the RSVP protocol number on exit.

The aggregator sends separate aggregate Path messages to the deaggregator, which replies with aggregate Resv messages. Traffic inside the region is classified by a Diff-Serv code point (DSCP), so routers can apply a forwarding treatment to a class of flows without examining each reservation.
sections.plainLanguage: The entrance router marks selected RSVP messages so routers in the middle ignore their reservation details. A DSCP marks the traffic class that uses the shared reservation.

sections.title: Creating and Using the Aggregate
sections.content:
When the deaggregator receives an E2E Path but has no aggregate Path for the required DSCP, it sends a PathErr with code NEW-AGGREGATE-NEEDED and the DSCP in a DCLASS object. This is a request to the aggregator, not a fatal error. The aggregator then creates the aggregate Path.

When the E2E Resv arrives, the deaggregator checks whether the aggregate reservation has enough bandwidth. It may increase or create the aggregate reservation, then forwards the E2E Resv with the selected DSCP. The aggregator records that mapping and marks matching data with the appropriate DSCP. Each E2E flow is policed against its own token bucket.

When an E2E reservation ends, its resource requirements are removed from the aggregate. If the aggregate itself ends, the E2E reservations it supports are no longer active.
sections.plainLanguage: The exit asks for a shared reservation if one does not yet exist. It checks capacity before assigning a new flow and tells the entrance which traffic marking to use.

sections.title: Sizing the Shared Reservation
sections.content:
The aggregate reservation must provide enough bandwidth and burst capacity for its E2E reservations. Resizing it every time one flow changes would increase message processing and reduce the benefit of aggregation.

The RFC therefore leaves sizing policy to the operator and suggests estimating future demand from known patterns and recent trends. It recommends making changes infrequently and using hysteresis so the reservation does not repeatedly grow and shrink.
sections.plainLanguage: The shared reservation needs enough capacity for the flows using it. Operators can estimate demand and adjust the reservation less often than every individual flow changes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Loss of an aggregate reservation can leave many calls unreserved, while reserving too much bandwidth can cause denial of service. The RFC notes that these risks also exist in RSVP itself.

A risk specific to aggregation is malicious alteration of the IP protocol number that marks E2E messages for interior routers to ignore. The RFC suggests IPsec authentication as a mitigation and recommends limiting protocol-number changes to Path, PathTear and ResvConf messages.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker who changes the protocol number in a message could stop a reservation from being established. The RFC recommends restricting which messages implementations may modify.
